cues.text: Before an agent hands out its email address for verification codes or receipts, it needs to know one thing.
Does this mailbox actually deliver mail, end to end?
The Mermail Inbox Canary skill answers that with one tagged probe and a verdict grounded only in real tool results.
This is a real run against hosted Mermail. The round trip could not be verified — and the runner’s own verdict had to be withdrawn.
The request it serves looks like this:
“Use Mermail to prove my agent mailbox can send and receive mail before I hand the address to a service.”
The run used the real hosted Mermail MCP server through an authenticated session.
Captured log: server mermail 1.0.0 · protocol 2025-06-18 · catalog: 94 tools.
send_email is present, which the probe needs. The agent-inbox profile lacks it, so the skill never runs a canary there.
list_workspaces + list_mailboxes resolved one ready owner inbox: tokenjunkielabs@mermail.app (public_id e48c62aa…).
Before anything is sent, the probe plan is journaled: a unique token, and the same mailbox as sender and recipient.
planned_send_at 2026-10-07T10:51:25.521Z · token mc-20261007-fq450to1
Then exactly one send_email call — approved via --approve-send by the operator.
sent_at 10:51:26.827Z (+1.306 s after the plan) · id d1658608… · status queued · undo_until 10:51:38.363Z.
Everything in this video comes from that one recorded run. Nothing was sent again to make it.
Next, the runner ran one bounded search_emails poll on the receiving mailbox: metadata only, held messages included.
Poll after +5 s: candidates=1 total=1.
But a search hit is only a candidate. It still has to pass validation before it counts as an arrival.
Here is the catch with a self-probe: the token can appear on two different messages — the copy that was sent and, if delivery works, the copy that is received.
Searching by token alone can surface both.
Every recorded read returned the same single message: d1658608… — the send receipt’s own id, folder_id "sent".
Reads at 10:52:50Z and 10:55:23Z: delivery_status "delivered", folder Sent, totalCount 1.
That proves the outgoing leg. It proves nothing about arrival.
No distinct incoming copy was observed.
And this is exactly where the runner’s own verdict went wrong.
Its log called it “the arrived probe” — but the record says folder_id "sent", delivery_status "queued".
It reported “degraded — round-trip 6.5s” from the date field: a record date, not a receipt.
That result is withdrawn, and it is never used as inbox proof.
The matcher was then tightened: it rejects the send receipt’s own id, Sent/Outbox folders and queued status, and requires an inbound marker.
That repair has only been exercised on a synthetic case, so it is not presented as provider evidence.
For this run: the token matches, but the id is the send receipt’s own, and the folder is Sent.
sender_authentication: unknown (reason: inbound_provider_unavailable) · scan_status: null.
Judged by those rules: zero validating candidates inside the bounded window.
Authoritative: OUTBOUND DELIVERED · INBOUND NOT OBSERVED · ROUND-TRIP LATENCY UNAVAILABLE.
In the record: inbound_message_id null · round_trip_latency null.
This is not a healthy result, and it is not reported as one.
The skill’s own rule — which the runner’s verdict broke: “Never claim the probe arrived on the basis of a send success or a pending state.”
This summary, composed from the records, names the mailbox and its public_id, the probe token, and the outgoing message id.
The skill never deletes or moves the probe automatically — its id is reported so the owner can handle it.
The stage that could not be verified is receive. Any re-check needs a fresh, approved probe — never an automatic resend.
The skill is open for review: github.com/Nudgen-Marketing/mermail-skills/pull/498
